An Ice Age story

Before our time, giants ruled.

Step into the lost world of the woolly mammoth. Discover the remarkable animal that roamed the Ice Age, the landscapes it called home, and the evidence it left behind.

01 / Meet the mammoth

More than a giant. A survivor of another world.

The woolly mammoth was built for life in cold environments. Its thick coat, insulating body fat, and distinctive tusks helped it survive across the northern regions of the Ice Age world.

Its story is preserved in fossils, teeth, bones, and, in rare cases, remarkably preserved remains.

02 / Anatomy & adaptation

Every detail had a purpose.

From its insulating coat to its powerful molars, the woolly mammoth carried a set of adaptations suited to the environments in which it lived.

Artistic reconstruction. Molars sit inside the jaw; marker 03 points to the mouth region.

    03 / The Ice Age world

    A world of grass, wind, and ice.

    Artistic reconstruction of a mammoth herd.

    The woolly mammoth inhabited cold northern environments shaped by changing climates. Much of its world included open, productive grassland known as the mammoth steppe.

    These landscapes supported large herbivores and the ecosystems connected to them.

    These are broad regional notes, not exact range boundaries. The range changed over time, and sea level and ice sheets reshaped the land.

    04 / A species through time

    Its story spans millions of years.

    The woolly mammoth was part of a much longer mammoth lineage. Its evolution, expansion, and eventual decline unfolded across changing environments and thousands of generations.

    Dates are approximate and sources differ. Images are artistic reconstructions or museum mounts. Not all mammoth species lived at the same time.

    05 / The disappearance

    When the world changed, their future changed with it.

    As the Ice Age ended, climates and habitats shifted. Human activity also formed part of the pressures facing mammoth populations.

    Their disappearance was not a single event shared by every population. Different groups survived for different lengths of time, and the causes of their decline involved multiple interacting factors.

    What the evidence tells us

      Extinction is rarely a simple story.

      06 / Evidence from the past

      The past leaves traces.

      Bones, teeth, preserved remains, and ancient DNA allow researchers to investigate how mammoths lived, changed, and disappeared.

      Each discovery adds another piece to a story that cannot be reconstructed from any single specimen.

      07 / Ancient life, modern science

      Could a giant ever return?

      Advances in genetics have opened new ways to study extinct animals and their living relatives.

      Research exploring mammoth-like traits raises questions about genetics, conservation, animal welfare, and the limits of what science can recreate.

      A living elephant engineered to express selected mammoth-like traits would not simply be a resurrected woolly mammoth.
